clinicalPearls: Anti-amphiphysin targets amphiphysin, a presynaptic protein involved in synaptic vesicle endocytosis.
It is most strongly associated with breast carcinoma in women and with small cell lung carcinoma.
The best-recognised phenotype is paraneoplastic stiff-person syndrome, which more often involves the neck and arms and shows a broader distribution than classic anti-GAD stiff-person syndrome.
Other presentations include encephalomyelitis, sensory neuronopathy, myelopathy and a mixed sensorimotor neuropathy.
Muscle rigidity with painful spasms, exaggerated startle and stimulus-sensitive spasms are characteristic of the stiff-person phenotype.
Anti-amphiphysin frequently coexists with anti-CV2/CRMP5 or anti-Hu, expanding the clinical and tumour spectrum.
Unlike anti-GAD stiff-person syndrome, the anti-amphiphysin form is paraneoplastic, so identifying and treating the tumour is central to management.
Electromyography during spasms shows continuous motor unit activity with co-contraction of agonist and antagonist muscles.
reference.pathophysiology: Amphiphysin is a presynaptic protein that participates in clathrin-mediated synaptic vesicle endocytosis and recycling, and it is enriched at inhibitory GABAergic and other synaptic terminals. Breast carcinoma and small cell lung carcinoma that ectopically express amphiphysin drive an onconeural immune response, generating the antibody as a diagnostic marker. In the stiff-person phenotype, impaired GABAergic inhibitory signalling is thought to underlie the axial and limb rigidity and stimulus-sensitive spasms, and passive transfer studies suggest a contribution of antibody to inhibitory synaptic dysfunction. Because amphiphysin is an intracellular antigen, cytotoxic T-cell mechanisms are also implicated, particularly in the encephalomyelitis and sensory neuronopathy variants, producing widespread involvement across the central and peripheral nervous systems.
additionalDifferentials: Anti-GAD65 stiff-person syndrome, which is usually non-paraneoplastic
Anti-glycine receptor antibody disease and progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
Other onconeural antibody syndromes such as anti-CV2/CRMP5 or anti-Hu, which may coexist
Dystonia, spasticity from structural myelopathy, or acquired neuromyotonia
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid anti-amphiphysin with confirmatory assays and a panel for coexisting onconeural antibodies
Testing for anti-GAD65 and anti-glycine receptor antibodies to distinguish related syndromes
Mammography, breast MRI, and CT of the chest with whole-body FDG-PET for breast or small cell lung carcinoma
Electromyography demonstrating continuous motor unit activity and agonist-antagonist co-contraction
MRI of the brain and spinal cord to assess encephalomyelitis or myelopathy
Nerve conduction studies where neuropathy or sensory neuronopathy is suspected
Cerebrospinal fluid for pleocytosis, raised protein and oligoclonal bands
redFlags: Severe truncal and respiratory muscle spasms compromising ventilation
Stimulus-sensitive spasms causing falls, fractures or joint dislocation
Occult breast or lung malignancy requiring urgent staging
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying tumour and the specific neurological phenotype; the stiff-person phenotype may respond partially to tumour treatment combined with GABA-enhancing and immunotherapies, whereas encephalomyelitis and neuronopathy variants carry a poorer outlook.
pitfalls: Assuming stiff-person syndrome is anti-GAD related and missing the paraneoplastic anti-amphiphysin cause
Failing to search for breast or lung cancer once the antibody is identified
Overlooking coexisting onconeural antibodies that change the tumour association
Misdiagnosing spasms as functional or psychogenic
Neglecting airway and respiratory monitoring during severe spasms
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
Consensus diagnostic criteria for paraneoplastic neurological syndromes
